item.title: Bank of Canada keeps 2% inflation target in mandate renewal
item.description: The Bank of Canada and federal government have agreed to keep a target of two per cent inflation at the core of the central bank’s mandate.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: OTTAWA — The Bank of Canada and federal government have agreed to keep a target of two per cent inflation at the core of the central bank’s mandate. The Bank of Canada sets its benchmark interest rate independently from the federal government but it gets its inflation-targetting mandate from Ottawa. The Bank of Canada said in a release announcing the renewal of its five-year mandate today that its inflation target has served Canadians well in recent decades. The central bank will continue to set monetary policy to make sure annual inflation dips neither too far below or above two per cent, but it retains flexibility to respond to economic shocks. The Bank of Canada increased its benchmark interest rate for the first time in three years last week as monetary policymakers fear inflationary pressures could start to spread. The bank announced the mandate renewal minutes after the federal Liberals outlined its economic projections and fiscal track in Budget 2026 on Thursday. --- Craig Lord, The Canadian Press This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 5, 2026.

item.title: Six smaller things in Budget 2026 that will affect Canadians
item.description: Alongside the big-ticket items in the federal budget, there are some perks for artists, hockey players and those who send mail the old- fashioned way. Here are six things you need to know right now.
item.dc:creator: Graham Richardson
item.content:encoded: Alongside the big-ticket items in the federal budget, there are some perks for artists, hockey players and those who send mail the old- fashioned way. Here are six things you need to know right now. 1) Stamp prices jump nearly 40 per cent Trying to stem losses at Canada Post, the Crown corporation will increase the price of a stamp from $1.44 to $2, a jump of nearly 40 per cent. Stamp prices will then rise by seven per cent annually. 2) Free admission to national museums for people under 25 The government is renewing the Canada Strong Pass, which provides free access to national museums for people under the age of 25. Extending the program to institutions including the Canadian Museum of History, the Canadian Museum of Nature, the Canadian Museum for Human Rights and the National Gallery of Canada will cost more than $500 million over the next five years. 3) Billions for rinks and recreation centres The federal government is earmarking $1.5 billion over nine years for recreational facilities, including $750 million for ice rinks and $750 million for recreation centres. “We will also revitalize the arenas and rinks where generations of Canadians have learned to skate, play, and dream,” Finance Minister Francois-Phillippe Champagne said in prepared remarks from his budget speech. 4) New tax credit for artists The budget introduces additional tax relief for artists through a new Canada Creative Credit. The government says artists could claim up to $45,000 in non-refundable personal income tax credits when combined with the basic personal exemption. Ottawa says the measure is intended to support artists and foster creativity. 5) Tax debts could affect credit ratings Canadians who owe more than $50,000 to the Canada Revenue Agency could see their credit ratings affected. The government plans to amend the Income Tax Act to allow the CRA to report tax debts above that threshold to credit reporting agencies. 6) GST/HST exemption for massage therapists Massage therapists will no longer be required to charge GST/HST on their services under a new tax exemption included in the budget.

item.title: Average asking rents fall 3.2% in October but prices rising in Toronto, Vancouver
item.description: The average asking price for a rental unit across Canada in October was $2,036, down 3.2 per cent compared with a year ago.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: TORONTO — The average asking price for a rental unit across Canada in October was $2,036, down 3.2 per cent compared with a year ago. A monthly report from Rentals.ca and Urbanation says October’s decrease marks the smallest year-over-year decline since February, when rents were down 2.8 per cent from the same month a year earlier. Average asking rents have now fallen year-over-year for 25 consecutive months, with prices down 5.4 per cent compared with two years ago and reaching their lowest October level since 2022. Rents were essentially flat on a monthly basis, edging 0.1 per cent higher from September. Urbanation president Shaun Hildebrand says the window for cheaper rents is closing in Toronto and Vancouver as prices are starting to rise for the first time in nearly three years amid declining supply, while renters still hold the advantage in Calgary, Edmonton and much of Ontario, where prices continue to fall. Asking rents for purpose-built apartments fell 2.1 per cent year-over-year to an average of $2,040 last month, while asking rents for condominium apartments decreased 5.5 per cent to $2,048. --- This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 5, 2026.

item.title: Nutrien sees strong potash demand, weakness in pricey nitrogen fertilizer
item.description: Nutrien is struggling from fertilizer production challenges affecting the industry globally, posting quarterly earnings below analyst estimates as a slump in nitrogen fertilizer sales and increased ...
item.dc:creator: Reuters Staff
item.content:encoded: WINNIPEG -- Nutrien is struggling from fertilizer production challenges affecting the industry globally, posting quarterly earnings below analyst estimates as a slump in nitrogen fertilizer sales and increased sulfur and other production costs drag on profitability. The world’s largest potash producer reported on Thursday third-quarter earnings of 61 cents per share compared to expectations of 80 cents a share. In its results conference call, the Saskatoon-based company said it is seeing financially squeezed farmers, especially in Brazil, putting off nitrogen fertilizer purchases, but global demand remaining high for potash, its main product. It expects U.S. farmers to catch up with their fall fertilizer applications in coming weeks due to better recent weather and the need to replenish soils drained by this year’s crop. The company will close its Florida phosphate fertilizer mine and processing in the first half of 2027 due to poor profitability and depleting reserves, and has now finished closing its Trinidad nitrogen fertilizer plant due to unsure natural gas supply and issues with port charges. It is retaining and reinvesting in its more efficient Aurora, North Carolina phosphate mine and complex, which it had also been considering selling. President and Chief Executive Ken Seitz said that having production located in North America is an advantage over producers in regions like Europe, which have far higher natural gas costs. “The competitive advantages are extraordinary,” Seitz said. “That gives us the confidence to invest, that gives us the confidence to unlock” more production. Despite high prices for nitrogen and phosphate fertilizers, high natural gas and sulfur prices have constrained margins for those products, spurring some companies to reduce production. Nutrien attributed falling nitrogen fertilizer and other product sales in Brazil to farmers running low on credit. The company expects Chinese demand to remain firm to ensure food security. (Reporting by Ed White and Khusbu Jena; Editing by Susan Fenton)
